reconcile.connective: Defenders deny any clash over duration: the Hebrew yom in Genesis 2:4 is the idiomatic "when," a summary covering the whole six-day week, not a rival one-day creation.

discrepancy.connective: Source critics, classically Julius Wellhausen, argue Genesis 2:4 belongs to a separate (J) account whose single-"day" framing was never meant to be squared with the six-day schema of the Priestly account in Genesis 1.

skeptic.name: Julius Wellhausen
skeptic.work: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
skeptic.attribution: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (Eng. trans. 1885; German 1883)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The Hebrew yom can refer to daylight (1:5a), to a 24-hour period (1:5b), or to an unspecified time period (2:4b, “When,” literally in the day; cp. Exod 20:8-11).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly distinguishes the senses of the very word at issue, stating that the 'day' of 2:4b is an unspecified time period ('When'), not the same as a 24-hour creation day — the precise hinge of the contradiction.

excerpts.excerpt_text: meaning not any particular day, not the first day, in which the heavens and the earth were created; but referring to the whole time of the six days, in which everything in them, and relating to them, were made.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads 'in the day' of Gen 2:4 as a summary of the whole six-day week rather than a single day, explicitly harmonizing the one-'day' wording with the six-day account.

pd_work.note: Gill's note on Gen 2:4 treats this passage directly, reading 'in the day' as the whole six-day creation period rather than a single day (Haley's specific coverage of this verse could not be confirmed, so a harmonizing commentator already on the row is used).
